sourceDesc.p: Trinity College, Cambridge, Dawson Turner Papers, Correspondence. The letter survives in an undated copy in an unknown hand, probably a member of the Turner family; it is endorsed ‘Original is among Autographs Series A’, and is placed after a copy of Mary Dawson Turner’s 1815 etching of Southey. TR; 2p. . Not previously published.
These letters were edited with the assistance of Tim Fulford, Ian Packer and Lynda Pratt

div.head:
2816. Robert Southey to Dawson Turner, 24 June 1816MS: Haverford College Quaker and Special Collections. An undated copy in an unknown hand, probably a member of the Turner family, is in Trinity College, Cambridge, Dawson Turner Papers, Correspondence, and endorsed ‘Original is among Autographs Series A’, and is placed after a copy of Mary Dawson Turner’s 1815 etching of Southey. TR; 2p.
Unpublished.
div.p: Your letter of the third, has reached me by this days post. I cannot but feel honoured by the compliment which Mrs TurnerMary Dawson Turner (1775–1850), a keen artist, particularly skilled in etching. She was tutored by John Crome (1768–1821; DNB) and later by John Sell Cotman (1782–1842; DNB). has paid me, & gratified by the manner in which you notice the recent loss of my son, Herbert Southey had died on 17 April 1816. You who have experienced the nature of such an afflictionThree of the Turners’ eleven children had died in infancy. (& none can tell what it is but those who have experienced it) know also that under such afflictions there is but one source of consolation. The loss which in its kind is common to all parents, has been in its degree peculiarly severe, because the boy was in every thing what my heart desired, – so entirely so, that I had often gazed upon him with the ominous feeling that he was fitter for a better world than this. In that world we shall meet, – & as this dispensation contributes to fix my heart & hopes more fervently upon a future state, I feel & acknowledge its use.

You will oblige Mrs Southey & myself if when an opportunity offers you will have the goodness to send a few impressions of the etchingMary Dawson Turner’s etching of Southey (1815). It was based on the portrait by Thomas Phillips (1770–1845; DNB) and is in the National Portrait Gallery. to my brother Dr Southey, 15. Queen Ann Street, Cavendish Square. The observations which my family make upon it are that the eye is too small, & that the eyebrow & forehead are both unlike: my forehead having no depression, & my eyebrows being remarkable regular. Every person here is struck with its resemblance to Bellingham,John Bellingham (1770–1812; DNB), who had assassinated Spencer Perceval in the lobby of the House of Commons in 11 May 1812. He was executed on 18 May 1812. of whom we possess a likeness etched by Dawe,George Dawe (1781–1829; DNB). Dawe had stayed at Greta Hall in autumn 1812 whilst he worked on the 9 foot by 8 foot canvas ‘Mother Rescuing her Child from an Eagle’s Nest’. The portrait owned by the Southeys was possibly Dawe’s pencil sketch ‘Study of John Bellingham’. – it was noticed at the time of this unhappy mans appearance before the public, that he was singularly like Sir Francis Burdett; & there is that sort of likeness between Sir Francis & myself, that my brother once purchased a caricature of Sir Francis supposing it had been designed for me.

Should any circumstances bring you & Mrs Turner to the Land of Lakes, I trust you will do me the favour of comparing the original with the portrait. Should I ever again visit the Eastern counties I will not fail to avail myself of your kind invitation.

closer.salute: Yours very thankfully & with sincere respect
